prompt: Write 10 distinct lessons the claims-triage agent (home and motor claims assessment within delegated authority) at Larkmere Mutual learned across many cases about: worried the house is in a flood zone. Each is a working pattern or tip for the next case, not about any one member, one or two sentences, in the agent's voice ("When…, …"). Return {"items": [{"type": "fact" | "preference" | "observation", "content": "..."}]} with exactly 10 items. (batch 1)
response: {"items":[{"type":"observation","content":"When a member says they are worried the house is in a flood zone, I check whether the concern is based on a recent event, a neighbour’s experience, or a map they have found online, because those usually need different reassurance and next steps."},{"type":"fact","content":"When the property is in an area with a known flood history, I treat the triage as higher risk even if no water has entered yet, because the likelihood of a weather-related claim can change quickly after heavy rain or warnings from the Met Office."},{"type":"preference","content":"When the member is anxious but there is no active flooding, I prefer to explain the difference between a flood risk area and an immediate claim situation, so the conversation stays calm and focused on practical checks."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the concern is about surface water rather than river flooding, I look for clues about drains, road levels, and previous rainwater issues, because the likely cause and urgency can be quite different."},{"type":"fact","content":"When a flood warning or severe weather alert is in place, I move faster on eligibility, safety advice, and evidence gathering, because timing matters more than in an ordinary home damage report."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the property has had previous water ingress but not from a flood source, I do not assume the new worry is the same problem, because escape of water, damp, and flood events need separate assessment."},{"type":"preference","content":"When the member can safely do so, I prefer to ask for clear photos of affected rooms, thresholds, gardens, and nearby water levels, because it helps me distinguish a genuine flood exposure from a precautionary concern."},{"type":"fact","content":"When there are signs of imminent flooding, I prioritise advice on safety, emergency services, and temporary protection over claim detail, because protecting people and the home comes before assessing loss."},{"type":"observation","content":"When the member mentions a lower-lying driveway, garden, or access road, I treat that as a useful indicator, because flood water often shows up there before it reaches the living areas."},{"type":"preference","content":"When the risk is uncertain, I prefer to note the concern carefully and signpost the member to local authority or Environment Agency style flood information rather than overstate certainty, because accurate wording avoids false reassurance or unnecessary alarm."}]}
